title: Patterns in the booking system
idea: Incorporating design patterns means placing a known structure exactly where your system expects change, so a new rule or reaction becomes a new class, not an edit.
points: `ConflictPolicy` is a Strategy: each overlap rule lives in its own class.
`BookingListener` is an Observer: email and audit react without `BookingService` knowing them.
Pick patterns from the change list in your requirements, never from a pattern catalogue.
In the interview, name each pattern, the change it absorbs, and its cost.

steps.caption: `BookingService` owns the booking flow. It depends on two interfaces, never on concrete rules or reactions.
Before saving, it asks a `ConflictPolicy` whether the candidate clashes with the room's bookings.
Each overlap rule is one Strategy class. The service is built with one of them.
Facilities asks for a cleaning gap. You add `CleaningGap`; `BookingService` stays untouched.
After saving, the service tells every registered `BookingListener`. It does not know who they are.
Email and audit are two Observers. A Slack alert would be a third class, not an edit.

code.title: The problem: rules in if/else
code.caption: Rules chosen by a mode string, reactions printed inline. A typo silently switches the rule off.

walk.text: The rule is picked by a free-form `String`. The compiler cannot check its value.
Every new rule adds an `else if` here, so this method changes for every policy request.
The overlap maths is mixed with the rule choice, so neither can be tested alone.
Email and audit are hard-coded. Adding a Slack alert means editing the booking method again.
`CLEANING-GAP` does not equal `CLEANING_GAP`, so the gap is 0 and the clash is accepted.

code.title: The fix: Strategy + Observer
code.caption: The same flow with a `ConflictPolicy` strategy and `BookingListener` observers injected through the constructor.

walk.text: Wiring happens once, at the edge. A wrong policy name is now a compile error.
The Strategy contract from the capstone spec. The service only knows this method.
One rule, one class. The compact constructor rejects a negative gap at creation time.
The Observer contract. Each listener does one job and can be tested with a fake booking.
Dependencies arrive through the constructor. `List.copyOf` stops callers adding listeners later.
Only this room's bookings go to the policy. A clash throws `RoomTakenException` with a stable code.
Listeners run only after the save, so a rejected booking never sends an email.

pitfalls: Adding a Factory or Builder nobody needs; reviewers ask which requirement it serves.
Notifying listeners before saving sends emails for bookings that later fail.
One throwing listener aborts the others; decide whether to catch per listener and log.

quiz.q: Some buildings need VIP rooms bookable only by managers. Which change fits this design best?
options: A new `BookingListener` that cancels non-manager VIP bookings
A new `ConflictPolicy` that rejects VIP slots for non-managers
A new `BookingPermission` interface that `book()` checks before the policy
quiz.why: A permission rule is not a time clash, so it needs its own extension point. A policy bends its contract; a listener acts too late; a subclass duplicates the flow.

takeaway: Put a pattern where the requirements predict change, and name that change.

starters: Should the repositories in the capstone also be behind interfaces?
